title: Work and Wages
tagline: Year 2 — Dividing payment in proportion to the work done

introduction.overview: When several workers complete a job together and are paid a total amount, each worker's fair share is proportional to the work they did. Work done is the product of rate and time, so the wage ratio is the ratio of (work done), not of the days worked unless the workers are equally efficient. This chapter builds on time-and-work rates to share money.
introduction.placementRelevance: Work and wages problems are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually as a short extension of a time-and-work problem.
introduction.realWorldContext: Paying contract labour, sharing a freelance fee among a team, and costing a project by man-days all use these ideas.

learningObjectives: Divide wages in the ratio of the work done
Find work done from rate and time
Handle workers who leave or join mid-job
Handle overtime and different daily rates

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Work done = rate × time. Workers who finish a job together share the pay in the ratio of the fractions of the job each did.

coreDefinitions: Wages: payment for work, usually proportional to work done.
Wage ratio: ratio of the shares of the total payment.
Man-day: one worker working for one day; the cost of a job = man-days × wage per man-day.
Efficiency: work per day; ratio of efficiencies = inverse ratio of times.
Overtime: extra hours paid at a higher rate.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Payment follows the work. If two workers work for the same time, the faster one has done more and earns more. If two workers have the same speed, the one who worked more days earns more. So the wage ratio is the ratio of (rate × time).
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: First find each worker's fraction of the job. Then the share of wages equals that fraction of the total pay. Fractions add up to 1 when the job is complete.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Wage ratio
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: A 3 days, B 2 days at the same rate → 3 : 2

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Equal time, different speeds
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Wage ratio = ratio of rates = inverse ratio of days alone

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Late leaver
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Add the work done together to the work done alone
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: A leaves after 3 days → A : B = 1 : 4

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Overtime
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Pay = normal hours × rate + extra hours × overtime rate
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Overtime is paid at a multiple.

mainNarrative: Find the fraction of the job done by each worker. If A takes 12 days and B takes 18 days and they work together for the whole job, A does 18/(12 + 18) = 3/5... more simply, the ratio of their rates is 1/12 : 1/18 = 3 : 2, so A gets 3/5 of the wages.

When both work for the same time, the wage ratio equals the ratio of their efficiencies. If three workers take 10, 15 and 30 days alone, their rates are 3 : 2 : 1 (on a base of 30 units). A ₹3,000 job is split ₹1,500, ₹1,000 and ₹500.

If a worker leaves midway, compute the work in two phases. A (15 days) and B (20 days) work 3 days together, then A leaves and B finishes. A does 3/15 = 1/5. B does 3/20 together and then the remaining 13/20, a total of 4/5. So A : B = 1 : 4.
To cost a job by man-days, find the wage per man-day. If 25 men working 12 days cost ₹9,000, then the cost per man-day is 9000 ÷ 300 = ₹30.
Overtime: for 11 hours a day, a worker paid ₹60 per hour for 8 hours and 1.5 times for the extra hours earns 8 × 60 + 3 × 90 = ₹750 per day.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why not just days?
deepDiveAspects.content: Two workers can work the same number of days but at different speeds. Sharing by days alone is correct only when speeds are equal.

deepDiveAspects.title: Third helper
deepDiveAspects.content: If A and B take 6 and 8 days and the three together take 3 days, then C's rate is 1/3 − 1/6 − 1/8 = 1/24, so wages are in the ratio 4 : 3 : 1.

solvedExamples.title: Different speeds
solvedExamples.question: A can do a work in 12 days and B in 18 days. They finish a job together and are paid ₹6,000. How much does A receive?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Share in the ratio of rates.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: They worked the same number of days, so the faster worker did more.

solvedExamples.title: One worker leaves early
solvedExamples.question: A can do a work in 15 days and B in 20 days. They work together for 3 days, then A leaves and B finishes the work. The total pay is ₹3,500. Find A's share.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A did one-fifth of the whole job.

solvedExamples.title: Man-day cost
solvedExamples.question: 25 men working for 12 days are paid ₹9,000 in all. What is the cost for 20 men working for 15 days at the same rate?

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Compute the work of each worker in full fractions.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Convert days to units per day using the LCM, multiply by days worked and share the pay in that ratio.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Giving the larger share to the slower worker.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: The faster worker must have the larger share; the shares must add to the total.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Write units per day in a small table.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Contract-costing questions are common in applied aptitude tests.
